title: Sid Catlett's listening, shows and dancers
summary: Leeman first met Catlett with Louis Armstrong and watched him on 52nd Street; he admired his listening and his love of playing for tap dancers, as Leeman did for Barnet's revues.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, back to Sidney Catlett. I first met him when he was with Louis Armstrong's big band, had our association during his days with Louie's small band. And he was playing on 52nd Street also during the heydays when I was with Don Bias of the Three Deuces, he would be with Don at other times when I was possibly with Ben Webster, and later when I was with Ben Webster at the Famous Door, Sidney Catlett was with Don Bias. And when I was at the Famous Door with Ben Webster -- I must remember later on to tell you this, it's really a funny story.

So we became fast friends, Sidney and I, and I mentioned with whom and where he played so you can understand I had a long time and many chances to observe this man. A large man, well over six feet -- long arms, and extraordinary large hands. When he sat down at the drums, the drumsticks looked like toothpicks in his hand. You expected to hear a thunderous eruption from the drums. Instead, well, a soft, fluid flow of assorted sounds emanated.
Whatever the music called for -- let's put it that
way -- he listened, and that to me is the most important part of drumming, the listening; listening the soloist. Listen to what they're playing.

Sidney's timing was impeccable, his execution in taste predominated, and he had excellent training, basically, I'm sure, but we never discussed it. He played a swinging, awe inspiring show. He loved to play behind great tap dancers, lines of girls dancing -- and shows in general. He enjoyed playing them, as much as he did jazz runs. And some of that rubbed off on me, thank goodness, because with Barnett's band, I had to play many, many shows; theatres. The Apollo Theatre, Washington's Howard Theatre -- these are all black theatres, and we had black and white revues with Charlie Barnet , and there was a whole string of theatres that we played.

And all the greatest at that time, and we had the original Cotton Club boys and girls -- wonderful dancers, and we had comedians, Pigmeat Markum and Avis and Estraledis, stepbrothers, and to me the greatest of all dancers was Baby Lawrence, the greatest jazz dancer. I don't think anybody could disprove that. And Bunny Briggs, too -- Bunny Briggs was with us for a long time, stumping for some of the acts. There were some of the acts, among many.
And I enjoyed playing them. A good drummer could make an act really more exciting. I enjoyed that, I

know Sidney did, too. I admired and idolized his work, it was impeccable. You can't say enough or much more. He shaded his lows as the music demanded with such intense intuitiveness, it was almost uncanny. The drummer's drummer.
